summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing clients of the Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol.

eli5.summary: COPS lets network devices ask a policy server what to do. This gives tools a way to look at how those devices are doing.

subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and configuring the client side of the COPS policy protocol.

tldr.problem: A COPS client, the Policy Enforcement Point that asks a server for policy decisions, had no standard way for network management tools to monitor its connections or tell it where its servers are.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module with three groups: client capabilities, per-server status and statistics, and configuration of server addresses and the retry algorithm.
tldr.outcome: Management stations can read COPS client state and counters and configure server lists in a standard way. It covers only the client, not the server and not specific client-types.

today: RFC 2940 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It manages clients of the protocol in RFC 2748.

sections.title: The SNMP Framework and This MIB
sections.content:
RFC 2940 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing a client of the Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol. The module is written in SMIv2, the second version of the Structure of Management Information.

The RFC begins by listing the five components of the SNMP Management Framework: an architecture, the SMI for naming and describing objects, message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3), protocol operations, and a set of fundamental applications with access control. A MIB written in SMIv1 can be produced by translation, which must be semantically equivalent except where objects are omitted because no translation exists, for example a Counter64.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a standard way to ask network gadgets how they are doing. This memo adds a new set of questions, written in the standard format, for one kind of gadget.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
COPS is a client-server protocol for passing policy requests and decisions between a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), which acts as the COPS client, and a Policy Decision Point (PDP).

This MIB manages important features of a COPS client module. It supports monitoring of status and protocol statistics, and configuration of the client, in particular telling it where to find its servers. It does not manage a COPS server, and it does not manage specific COPS client-types such as the one used with RSVP. It describes a single COPS client represented by a single SNMP agent and one instance of the MIB-2 system group, and does not address several co-located clients.
sections.eli5: It is only about the helper, not the boss, and not the special jobs the helper might be doing. Just one helper per report card.

sections.title: Groups and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module is registered under mib-2 89, with objects arranged in three groups.

  • copsClientCapabilitiesGroup: the COPS capabilities this client implements, as one BITS object covering COPS version 1, IP-SEC AH, IP-SEC ESP, TLS and COPS Integrity.
  • copsClientStatusGroup: the current status of connections to COPS servers, with per-server protocol statistics. It keeps last-known statistics for every server connected since the agent restarted.
  • copsClientConfigGroup: configuration of server addresses and the order for trying connections, plus scalars for the retry algorithm.

Five textual conventions are defined: CopsClientState, CopsServerEntryType, CopsErrorCode, CopsTcpPort and CopsAuthType. They change neither syntax nor semantics of any object and exist for the convenience of readers. The error codes are identical to those of the COPS protocol itself.
sections.eli5: The report card has three pages: what the helper can do, how its calls are going, and the phone list. Some labels are just nicer names for plain numbers.

sections.title: The Status Table
sections.content:
copsClientServerCurrentTable describes COPS servers from the client's point of view. It holds both statically configured servers and ones learned dynamically through a PDP Redirect. Rows are indexed by server address type, server address and client-type. There is one entry for each client-type the server serves, plus an entry with client-type 0 that describes the underlying connection itself.

Each entry reports the TCP port, how the entry arose (copsServerStatic or copsServerRedirect), the authentication type in use and the time of the last connection attempt. It also reports the connection state, the Keepalive and Accounting timeouts in centiseconds (zero means no such activity), and a set of counters.

The client state takes six values: copsClientInvalid (1, the default), copsClientTcpconnected (2), copsClientAuthenticating (3), copsClientSecAccepted (4), copsClientAccepted (5) and copsClientTimingout (6).

The counters cover messages in and out, messages with syntax errors, the last error code, TCP connect and Client-Open attempts and failures, and specific problems such as unsupported client-type or version, length mismatch, unknown Op Code, C-Num or C-Type, wrong objects or Op Code, Keepalive timeouts, and authentication failures or missing authentication. They are cumulative since agent restart and are not zeroed on new connections.
sections.eli5: For each boss the helper talks to, there is a row showing how the connection is going and tally marks for messages sent, received and mistakes.

sections.title: Configuring Servers and Retries
sections.content:
copsClientServerConfigTable lists possible servers, indexed by address type, address, client-type and authentication type. The client tries them in priority order, and higher numbers are tried first. Order among equal priorities is undefined. There may be several entries for one server with different security mechanisms, tried in priority order. A server learned through PDP-Redirect always takes priority over any configured entry. Each row also has a TCP port and a RowStatus.

Three scalars control retries after a failed connection.

  • copsClientServerConfigRetryAlgrm: other (1), sequential (2) or roundRobin (3), defaulting to sequential.
  • copsClientServerConfigRetryCount: for sequential, how many times to retry one server before moving on; default 1. It is not used for round robin.
  • copsClientServerConfigRetryIntvl: in centiseconds; default 1000. For sequential it is the wait between retries to the same server. For round robin, the client tries each server in turn and, if all fail, waits this long before restarting.
sections.eli5: The phone list says which boss to call first. If nobody picks up, the helper either keeps trying the same one a few times or goes down the list and starts over after a wait.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content: Two groups of objects, copsDeviceStatusGroup and copsDeviceConfigGroup, are both mandatory under the compliance statement copsClientCompliance. The writable configuration objects (port, priority, row status, retry algorithm, count and interval) may be implemented read-only. Write access is required only if the device supports configuring COPS server information.
sections.eli5: A device must offer both the report card and the phone list, but it may let people only read the phone list if it does not support changing it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-create may be sensitive in some environments, and allowing SET operations without protection can harm network operations. SNMPv1 by itself is not secure. Even on a secure network, such as one using IPSec, there is no control over who may GET or SET the objects.

The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model. It is the customer's or user's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that only principals with legitimate rights can access the objects.
sections.eli5: Letting anyone change the phone list could cause trouble, so use the strong lock SNMPv3 offers and give keys only to people who should have them.
